newsitem.title: UK: Unionists in arms protest at N.Ireland talks.
newsitem.headline: Unionists in arms protest at N.Ireland talks.

text.p: Northern Ireland's pro-British Unionist parties walked out of Wednesday's session of Northern Ireland peace talks in a row over Anglo-Irish proposals to break deadlock on the surrender of guerrilla arms.

Spokesmen for the three parties said they were furious that Britain had resumed contact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to answer the party's queries about the issue even though it is banned from the negotiations because of IRA violence.

"If you shoot and if you bomb and if you throw petrol bombs....the government will jump through hoops to give you the clarification you desire," Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the hardline Democratic Unionist party (DUP) told reporters.

Britain broke off talks with Sinn Fein after the IRA ended a 17-month truce last year but resumed talks when the Labour party won May 1 elections. These were frozen again after the IRA murdered two policemen in a daylight ambush last month.
Unionists said they were furious at learning that the British government had been in contact with Sinn Fein to give it clarification about decommissioning and other issues.

The Unionist protest was aimed at Anglo-Irish plans that guerrillas surrender their weapons as the talks progress rather than before or after negotiations on a political settlement to a 28-year conflict that has killed 3,200.

So-called parallell decommissioning was proposed by talks chairman George Mitchell, a former U.S. Senator, and accepted by Britain and Ireland in an attempt to lure Sinn Fein to the talks and secure a new Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist party (UUP), the biggest in the province, said he was seeking urgent talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
"We have not got any clear definition of what parallell decommissioning means," Trimble complained.
The three parties said they would return when negotiations resume next Monday but were not optimistic they could vote for the proposals by the July 23 deadline Britain and Ireland set.

The two governments want the issue, which has snarled the year-long talks since day one, to be agreed so that the negotiations on a settlement between pro-British Protestants and pro-Irish Catholics can broach substantive issues in September.

Seamus Mallon of the Catholic-backed Social Democratic and Labour party said the protest was confined to three of eight parties taking part and hoped next week's vote would end the row over decommissioning.
He was sceptical that Unionist protest could force the breakdown of talks which Britain and Ireland say offer the best chance of a settlement for a generation.
He suggested that if the Unionists, who represent the 60 per cent Protestant population in Northern Ireland, did not accept the compromise, it should be put to a referendum.

Britain's minister of state, Paul Murphy, said he was disappointed by the walkout."Obviously I am disappointed if anyone goes away from the talks but if they reflect, they will be coming back next week," he told reporters.

Unionists fear the proposals are a sign of what they say is a determined effort to get their ideological foe, Sinn Fein, to the talks at any price, even if it means the party can negotiate while its guerrilla backers are still armed.

Ken Maginnis, security spokesman for the UUP said: "The government has not faced up to the reality of terrorist organisations armed to the teeth who have shown no willingness whatever to move into the democratic process and disarm."
Sinn Fein and the IRA have baulked at decommissioning. They say any arms handover should be the last item on the agenda after a political settlement is reached.
